title: Trading workflows, venues and counterparties

objectives.text: Trace an instruction through broker/venue/execution/post-trade roles while distinguishing order acknowledgment, fills, cancel confirmation and settlement.
Compare stated venue/execution alternatives on price, size, cost, latency and uncertainty without mistaking a quote or toy snapshot for guaranteed executable liquidity.

blocks.markdown: This module teaches market mechanics using synthetic single-currency stock/share examples, not a recommendation to trade or a claim about the user's broker. Sources include US securities-market education; specific legal obligations, permitted order types, tax/settlement cycles and access rules vary by jurisdiction, asset, venue and account. Do not apply a US example as an Indian or worldwide rule. Every real transaction needs its own current instrument/account/venue contract and authorization.

An investor or fund sends an instruction. A broker acts for a customer in arranging/executing a transaction; a dealer trades for its own account as principal. The same firm can perform both roles on different transactions, so identify capacity rather than inferring it from the brand. A market maker quotes buying/selling interest under its applicable arrangements and bears inventory/adverse-selection risk; earning a quoted spread is not a guaranteed profit. A venue is a place/system for trading under its rules, not automatically the customer's broker, custodian or legal counterparty.

Execution establishes a trade's price/quantity under its contract; clearing determines/processes obligations and may net/guarantee eligible trades; settlement transfers the required cash/securities through the applicable infrastructure. Custody/recordkeeping concerns holding assets and recording entitlements. In eligible centrally cleared systems, a clearing counterparty can interpose through novation, subject to acceptance/rules. This is not how every asset/OTC trade clears, and it does not remove all liquidity, operational, legal or default risk. DTCC's CNS is a concrete US service example, not a universal workflow.

blocks.title: Do not collapse different confirmations into one success flag

steps.text: A customer submits a request to buy 100 shares through a broker. Local send success records transmission, not venue acceptance or a trade.
The venue accepts the order. That acknowledgment may establish an order identifier/open quantity under the venue protocol, but no fill has occurred yet.

A confirmed execution for 30 shares leaves 70 open. The customer asks to cancel the remainder; before that request is processed, another 20 shares may execute. The cancel confirmation can then remove only 50 remaining shares.

The cumulative confirmed state is filled 50, canceled 50, open 0. The request to cancel 70 did not undo the extra 20 filled before cancellation. Trade obligations still need the applicable post-trade processing/settlement; a canceled remainder is not a reversal of existing trades.

blocks.caption: Expected dictionaries: {'filled': 0, 'canceled': 0, 'open': 100}; {'filled': 30, 'canceled': 0, 'open': 70}; {'filled': 50, 'canceled': 50, 'open': 0}; then inconsistent state rejected. The fixed requested quantity satisfies requested=filled+canceled+open. This helper checks a declared cumulative snapshot only; it does not authenticate events, detect duplicates/replaces/corrections or implement a broker protocol/state machine.

blocks.markdown: A displayed limit-order book exposes some priced interest and matches under a rulebook; an auction collects interest for a defined matching event; a dealer/request-for-quote interaction seeks a quoted trade from a counterparty. Listed instruments can trade through routes beyond one listing venue, and OTC does not mean one universal execution mechanism. These models can differ in transparency, liquidity, price formation, timing, size, access and counterparty/clearing arrangements. Do not label one globally best from a venue name alone.

Compare the same instrument, side, currency, settlement basis, order size and timestamp context. For a BUY, raw lower price is better all else equal, but fees and executable size matter. Quotes are for particular quantities and can change before arrival. Evaluate all-in expected cost, chance/size of fill, latency, information leakage, adverse selection and operational reliability under the strategy's constraints. A fee rebate alone or the fastest acknowledgment alone does not establish best execution or lowest total economic cost.

blocks.caption: Expected output: A (10050, Fraction(1005, 1)); B (10010, Fraction(1001, 1)); C None. Buying 10 shares at A costs 10000 cents plus 50 fee; B costs 10010 with no fee. Thus B is lower cost in this exact frozen full-fill fixture despite its worse quoted per-share price. C cannot fill the whole 10 at its displayed size 5 under the helper's no-splitting policy. No route is selected for a real order; changes/partial fills/hidden interest/cross-venue routing are excluded.

blocks.markdown: Keep client request IDs, broker/venue order IDs and execution IDs separate; their namespace/mapping comes from the protocol. The same-looking identifier from another account/venue need not be the same event. Event/exchange timestamp, receipt timestamp and processing sequence can differ. A missing or delayed response is not proof an order failed and safe to resubmit. Later modules implement sequence/idempotency state; here record uncertainty and reconcile authoritative reports instead of inventing a fill or duplicate order.

Track confirmed executions and open exposure separately. An unfilled order may still create future execution risk until cancellation is effective; settlement obligations can remain after the order is fully filled/canceled. Fees, settlement calendars, margin/short-sale rules, corporate actions, counterparty and legal terms require their actual current sources. This module deliberately does not teach a universal settlement day count, promise trade finality from an acknowledgment, or authorize a live order.

Independent transfer: annotate a timeline containing send, acknowledgment, partial fill, cancel request, another fill, cancel confirmation and settlement evidence. At each point state what is known and what remains uncertain, and reconcile share counts. Then compare two synthetic buy quotes including fees and limited displayed size. Name facts still missing before turning that comparison into an executable routing choice.

References: [SEC investor trade execution](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/how-stock-markets-work/executing-order), [FINRA broker/dealer roles](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/working-with-investment-professional/registered-financial-professionals), [confirmation capacity/fees](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/checking-trade-confirmations), and [DTCC CNS eligible clearing/novation/settlement](https://www.dtcc.com/products-and-services/clearing-settlement-services/equities-clearing/cns). US-specific examples are labeled, synthetic policies are not venue facts, and no brokerage capability is assumed.

summary: Order send, acceptance, execution, cancellation and settlement are distinct. Identify transaction roles/capacity and reconcile confirmed exposure; compare routes under explicit size/cost/time assumptions rather than assuming a quote or acknowledgment guarantees a fill.
